newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Islamist group claims Damascus bus bombing.
newsitem.headline: Islamist group claims Damascus bus bombing.

text.p: A Moslem militant group claimed responsibility on Thursday for a recent bus bombing in Syria, saying it was in retaliation for Syria's "execution" of one of its militants who took part in an attack on U.S. servicemen in Saudi Arabia last year.

The claim was made by a group calling itself the Islamic Movement for Change -- one of several previously unheard of organisations that said they carried out the bombing of a U.S.-run military training facility in the Saudi capital Riyadh in November, 1995.

"The group of martyr Sheikh Jaafar Bin Alhaj Qassem Marzouk al-Shwaikhat in the Jihad wing of the Islamic Movement For Change to Purge the Land of the Arab Peninsula has proved once again that its hand is long and has carried out the bombing operation of a Syrian military bus in the heart of Damascus, which led to the killing and injury of all its passengers," said a statement faxed to an international news agency in Nicosia.
The statement, in Arabic, could not be authenticated. It was not clear where it originated.

Syria said 11 people were killed and 42 wounded when a bomb exploded aboard a bus in central Damascus on December 31. Syria accused Israel of being behind the attack, an allegation that Israel quickly rejected.
The bus was a civilian vehicle on its way from Damascus to the northern city of Aleppo. Some of those on board were soldiers on leave.
In Damascus a senior Syrian official dismissed the claim of responsibility as a fake statement planted by Israel.
"These are suspicious statements aiming at diverting attention from Israel's responsibility for this criminal act," the official told Reuters.

The Islamic Movement for Change said it carried out the attack to avenge what it called Syria's execution of the "Mujahid" (holy warrior) Sheikh Jaafar Bin Alhaj Qassem Marzouk al-Shwaikhat who it said took part in the attack against a U.S. military base in Dhahran in eastern Saudi Arabia in June, 1996, in which 19 Americans were killed.
The group said al-Shwaikhat "had sought refuge in Syria seeking safety and security."
It was not clear whether this was the first time that Islamic Movement for Change had claimed responsibility for the Dhahran bombing.

The Washington Post last year quoted Saudi Interior Minister Prince Nayef as saying that al-Shwaikhat, said to be a Saudi Shi'ite member of the outlawed Islamist Saudi Hizbollah group, had been arrested by the Syrians at the request of Saudi authorities in connection with the Dhahran bombing but had died a few days later in a Syrian jail.
The Post said the Syrians told the Saudi investigators that he had committed suicide.
Nayef was said to have expressed the suspicion that a foreign government, believed to be Iran, had ordered his death to prevent him from disclosing any information about the bombing, it added.

Saudi Arabia has not disclosed the findings of its investigation into the June, 1996, attack in Dhahran but U.S. newspaper have reported that the finger of blame was pointing towards Iran -- an allegation denied by Tehran.
The Islamic Movement for Change accused Syrian President Hafez al-Assad of "betraying" Iran.

"We have remained silent for a long time on the attacks of the apostate Baath regime (in Syria) which has betrayed the Islamic republic of Iran one time after the other and joined the kings and petrol sheikhs in the Arab summit meetings...to condemn Iran, the guardian of Islam in the region and the world, and to oppose the installation of ground-to-ground Islamic Iranian missiles to protect the Arab Gulf from American and Zionist ambitions," the group said.
Syria was a close ally of Iran during the 1980-88 Iran-Iraq war but improved its ties with Gulf Arab states and the West by helping to oust Iraqi forces from Kuwait in 1991.
